What if the landlord does not provide a full refund, or a statement of deductions and a refund 
of amounts not deducted, by the end of the 21-day period as required by law? 
According to a California Supreme Court decision, the landlord loses the right to keep any of the 
security deposit and must r eturn the entire deposit to you. 380 
Even so, it may be difficult for you 
to get your entire deposit back from the landlord. 381 
The landlord may still claim damages for

In addition to limitations as to property type, just cause under the Tenant Protection Act applies 
only under certain conditions of tenure of the tenants. It applies if a tenancy has been in place for 
12 months or more. However, if any adult is added to occupancy in the unit before any tenant has 
resided there for 24 months, then the protection does not apply until all tenants have resided in 
the unit for 12 months or any tenant has resided there continuously for 24 months.334 
ADVANCE PAYMENT OF LAST MONTH’S RENT 
Many landlords require tenants to pay “last month’s rent” at the beginning of the tenancy as 
part of the security deposit or at the time the security deposit is paid. Almost without exception 
what a residential landlord calls “last month’s rent” is really nothing other than a security deposit. 
The security deposit law, Civil Code section 1950.5, places strict limits on the advance payment of 
rent and characterizes any money given to the landlord, except for an application fee and the first 
76 
month’s rent, as security deposit.335 
REFUND OF SECURITY DEPOSITS 
Common problems and how to avoid them 
One of the most common disagreements between landlords and tenants is over the refund of 
the tenant’s security deposit after the tenant has moved out of the rental unit. California law, 
therefore, specifies procedures that the landlord must follow for refunding, using, and accounting 
for tenants’ security deposits. 
California law specifically allows the landlord to use a tenant’s security deposit for four  
purposes: 
• For unpaid rent;
• For cleaning the rental unit when the tenant moves out, but only to make the unit as clean
as it was when the tenant first moved in, exclusive of normal wear and tear; 336
• For repair of damages, other than normal wear and tear, caused by the tenant or the
tenant’s guests; and
• If the rental agreement allows it, for the cost of restoring or replacing furniture, furnishings,
or other items of personal property (including keys), other than because of normal wear
and tear. 337

The rental-housing document collection does not provide specific information about the FTC's reported scale of rental-scam losses. However, it does provide information about California security-deposit limits, which include:

* Limits on the amount of the security deposit that the landlord can require (pages 34-36)
* The Tenant Protection Act, which places a cap on annual rent increases equal to 5% plus inflation, or 10%, whichever is lower, and no more than two rental increases within a 12-month period (pages 39-40)
* Limits on the landlord's right to enter the rental unit (pages 48-50)
* The right to a refund of the security deposit, or a written accounting of how any of it was used by the landlord, after you move out (pages 75-78)
* Other rights and protections for tenants, such as the right to sue the landlord for violations of the law, the right to repair serious defects in the rental unit, and the right to withhold rent under appropriate circumstances (pages 60-63, 58-59, and 60-63, respectively).

It's worth noting that the document collection does not provide information about the FTC's reported scale of rental-scam losses, which is not relevant to the information provided about California security-deposit limits.
